query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr-containing, FCC high-entropy alloys initially engineered as single-phase solid solutions (e.g., near-equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni), exposure to intermediate service temperatures (≈450–650°C) for engineering-relevant durations induces nanoscale short-range order (SRO) within grains and Cr-rich grain-boundary (GB) precipitation (e.g., sigma/Laves-like), which together reduce GB cohesive strength and promote planar slip with dislocation pile-up. Under subsequent mechanical loading, this microstructural evolution shifts fracture from ductile transgranular to intergranular/quasi-cleavage and measurably lowers fracture toughness and impact energy relative to the as-homogenized baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase solid-solution FCC high-entropy alloy with equiatomic or near-equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni composition (Cantor-type), homogenized/solutionized to suppress second phases; recrystallized grain size in the 10–100 µm range; negligible prior cold work; no intentional GB precipitates; tested in ambient air.
generation.intervention: Service-relevant thermal exposure (isothermal aging at 550°C for 100 h, representative of intermediate-temperature service), followed by monotonic mechanical loading (fracture toughness and impact tests) at room temperature.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure in air at 550°C; mechanical testing at 20–25°C in air under quasi-static loading rates for K_IC/J_IC and standard Charpy V-notch impact; specimens with identical geometry and surface finish; no hydrogen charging or corrosive environment to isolate the proposed mechanism.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary precipitation/segregation of Cr-rich intermetallics (sigma/Laves-like) and intragranular chemical short-range order (SRO)/clustering that increases lattice friction and promotes planar slip; local GB depletion/enrichment patterns that lower GB cohesive energy.
generation.mechanism: Intermediate-temperature exposure drives partitioning of Cr (and possibly Mo if present) to GBs, forming brittle GB precipitates and/or segregation layers that reduce GB cohesion. Concurrently, SRO within the FCC matrix raises the Peierls stress and promotes planar slip, reducing strain hardening and concentrating stress at GBs via dislocation pile-ups. Under mechanical loading, cracks initiate and propagate preferentially along embrittled GBs or via quasi-cleavage, reducing toughness relative to the single-phase baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-homogenized baseline: (1) lower measured fracture toughness (K_IC/J_IC) and Charpy impact energy after 550°C aging; (2) increased fraction of intergranular/quasi-cleavage features in fractography; (3) detection of GB precipitates/segregation and SRO signatures (e.g., by TEM/APT and diffuse scattering). Direction of changes is expected (embrittlement and more brittle fracture modes); the exact magnitudes are uncertain and depend on alloy chemistry, grain size, and exposure time.
generation.baseline: As-homogenized, single-phase FCC alloy tested at the same temperature and loading rates without prior aging, exhibiting ductile transgranular fracture with higher toughness and impact energy.
generation.boundary: Applies to Cr-containing FCC HEAs with propensity for GB phase formation/SRO under 450–650°C exposure for tens to hundreds of hours. Effects may be minimal for alloys deliberately designed to suppress GB precipitation (e.g., via chemistry or high GB fraction of special boundaries), for very short exposures or lower temperatures (<400°C), or for conditions dominated by other mechanisms (e.g., hydrogen embrittlement, cryogenic TWIP/TRIP). Grain size, minor alloying additions (e.g., Mo, C), and environment can shift the threshold.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of toughness/impact energy reduction is uncertain without alloy-specific diffusion/precipitation kinetics; specific phase identity (sigma vs Laves vs B2) depends on precise chemistry and exposure history. If the alloy strongly resists GB precipitation or SRO at the stated conditions, embrittlement may be weak or absent.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two cohorts from the same heat with identical processing: (A) baseline as-homogenized single-phase FCC specimens; (B) aged specimens exposed at 550°C for 100 h in air. Perform: (1) microstructural characterization pre- and post-aging (TEM, STEM-EDS, APT for GB chemistry and precipitates; XRD/TEM diffuse scattering or electron diffraction for SRO; EBSD for fracture path); (2) mechanical testing (K_IC or J_IC per ASTM standards and Charpy V-notch impact at room temperature); (3) fractography (SEM) to quantify intergranular vs transgranular fracture fractions. Maintain identical specimen geometry, loading rate, and environment.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC or J_IC) with statistical replication
Charpy V-notch impact energy at room temperature
Fraction of intergranular/quasi-cleavage features from fractography
GB precipitate volume fraction/coverage and chemistry by TEM/APT
Evidence of intragranular SRO (diffuse scattering or local compositional ordering by APT)
Dislocation slip character (planar vs wavy) by TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, after aging at 550°C for 100 h: (i) no GB precipitates/segregation and no SRO signatures are detected within measurement sensitivity, and toughness/impact energy and fracture mode do not differ from the baseline beyond statistical uncertainty; or (ii) GB precipitates/SRO are present, but fracture remains predominantly ductile transgranular with no statistically significant reduction in toughness/impact energy relative to baseline.
